## Revision Status: September 7, 2026

This review addresses the [historical reference](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/c270ea67fa94c96e4d1a6c441bc5965d3a75a4a4/articles/tangent-hyperplane-articles/Advanced/Contraction_Tangent_Unification.qmd) and corrects errors in the [earlier critique](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/3ccd69daa7c0d53ab31e7432c88fd846269a8ba2/articles/tangent-hyperplane-articles/Advanced/Contraction_Tangent_CRITIC.qmd). The [revised reference](Contraction_Tangent_Unification.html) already replaces the original unsupported theorems and experimental tables. Historical criticisms below are not allegations that those withdrawn claims remain in that edition.

The earlier critique identified real gaps but proposed several incorrect mathematical repairs and supplied invented replacement results. This version withdraws those proposed results, derives the applicable statements, and distinguishes a mathematical certificate from a research hypothesis. No robot or golfer experiment is reported here.
:::

## What the Investigation Needs to Establish

A golf swing is a brief, constrained motion whose success depends heavily on the state delivered at impact. The model must explain how preparation, geometry, inertia, muscle forces, shaft response and contact make that delivery possible. It must also explain which deviations can be corrected, which are tolerated, and which remain consequential when time runs out.

Contraction analysis addresses a particular part of that problem: whether neighboring solutions approach each other in a declared metric under a specified input policy. Optimal control addresses another: which admissible policy minimizes a declared cost. An experiment asks whether either description predicts measured behavior. A valid connection among these questions is useful; collapsing them into a single claim makes the argument harder to test.

The original reference overextended the connection. The earlier critique sometimes overcorrected in the opposite direction, treating time-varying metrics or coordinate expressions as inherently suspect. They are legitimate tools. The appropriate review asks whether the correct derivative, positive-definiteness conditions, domain, constraints and empirical interpretation are supplied.

The following sections preserve that review agenda while replacing its faulty reasoning. All numerical examples are constructed mathematical examples unless explicitly attributed to a primary study.

## The Riccati Connection Requires the Closed Loop {#weakness-1-the-duality-is-unidirectional-not-bidirectional}

### Derive the Identity Before Interpreting It

Consider the continuous-time linear system and finite-horizon cost
$$
\dot x=A(t)x+B(t)u,
$$
$$
J=x(T)^\top Q_Tx(T)
+\int_0^T\left(x^\top Qx+u^\top Ru\right)dt,
$$
with symmetric $Q,Q_T\succeq0$ and $R\succ0$. The unconstrained linear-quadratic solution has value $x^\top S(t)x$ and feedback $u=-Kx$, where
$$
\begin{aligned}
K&=R^{-1}B^\top S,\\
-\dot S&=A^\top S+SA-SBR^{-1}B^\top S+Q.
\end{aligned}
$$
These are the standard [finite-horizon LQR equations](https://underactuated.mit.edu/lqr.html). Here $A$ is the plant matrix. The actual closed-loop matrix is $A_c=A-BK$.

For the differential squared length $V=\delta x^\top S\delta x$, substitution gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot V
&=\delta x^\top\left(\dot S+A_c^\top S+SA_c\right)\delta x,\\
\dot S+A_c^\top S+SA_c
&=-Q-K^\top RK.
\end{aligned}
$$
This is an identity, not an approximation. The earlier critique inserted the open-loop $A$ into the metric test, obtained a different expression, and then changed a sign when rearranging it. That calculation did not test the feedback system it purported to assess.

The identity becomes a positive-rate contraction certificate only with additional conditions. On the stated time interval, require
$$
0<c_1I\preceq S(t)\preceq c_2I,
\qquad Q+K^\top RK\succeq2\lambda S,
$$
for a uniform $\lambda>0$. Then $\dot V\leq-2\lambda V$. Positive semidefinite cost weights alone do not provide these conditions.

At each time with $S\succ0$, the sharp rate available from this quadratic inequality is
$$
\lambda_*(t)=\frac12\lambda_{\min}
\left(S^{-1/2}(Q+K^\top RK)S^{-1/2}\right).
$$
A simpler sufficient bound is
$$
\lambda_*(t)\geq
\frac{\lambda_{\min}(Q+K^\top RK)}{2\lambda_{\max}(S)}.
$$
Use the infimum over the interval to claim a uniform rate. This is a generalized metric comparison; raw eigenvalues of $A_c$ do not replace it for a time-varying or nonnormal system. The rate has units of inverse time after the state coordinates and cost units have been fixed.

For infinite-horizon time-invariant LQR, stabilizability and detectability are familiar sufficient hypotheses for the stabilizing semidefinite Riccati solution under the usual nonnegative state-cost assumptions. They should not be stated as universal necessary conditions for every algebraic solution. Strict definiteness and a positive lower bound in the displayed metric inequality must still be checked if the value matrix itself is used to claim contraction.

### A Terminal Value Matrix Can Fail to Be a Metric

Take the finite-horizon scalar problem $\dot x=0$, $Q=1$, no effective control input, and $Q_T=0$. Its value is
$$
S(t)=T-t,\qquad x(t)=x(0).
$$
The value decreases because less running cost remains to be accumulated. The state does not converge, and $S(T)=0$ is not a metric. This example refutes the statement that every finite-horizon LQR value matrix certifies state contraction. It does not undermine finite-horizon optimal control.

On a compact interval, continuity and positive definiteness everywhere imply uniform eigenvalue bounds. Positive semidefiniteness at a terminal point does not. Choosing numerically well-conditioned $Q$ and $R$ alone cannot repair a zero terminal value matrix.

### The Earlier Inverse-Optimal Counterexample Was Not a Counterexample

For the stable matrix
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\0&-3\end{bmatrix},
\qquad M_1=I,\qquad M_2=\operatorname{diag}(2,1),
$$
both $A^\top M_i+M_iA$ are negative definite. With $B=0$, each produces a valid positive running-cost matrix $Q_i=-(A^\top M_i+M_iA)$. In particular,
$$
Q_2=\begin{bmatrix}8&-2\\-2&6\end{bmatrix},
\qquad\operatorname{eig}(Q_2)=7\pm\sqrt5.
$$
Thus the negative matrix has eigenvalues approximately $-9.236$ and $-4.764$, not the values printed in the earlier critique. The construction demonstrates nonuniqueness of the cost interpretation. It does not demonstrate nonexistence.

More generally, for a fixed open-loop matrix $A$ contracting in $M$, any chosen $B$ and $R\succ0$ yield
$$
Q=-(A^\top M+MA)+MBR^{-1}B^\top M\succ0.
$$
Then $M$ satisfies the algebraic Riccati equation for that constructed cost, and $K=R^{-1}B^\top M$ is the associated feedback. The resulting controlled dynamics differ from the original open-loop dynamics. This freedom to choose a cost is distinct from validating a predeclared biomechanical objective or a measured human policy.

A prescribed feedback can fail the stationarity condition. For $\dot x=-x+u$, let $u=-Kx$ with $K=-1/2$ and choose $M=1$. The closed loop is $\dot x=-x/2$, which contracts. But the ordinary LQR condition $RK=B^\top M$ would require $R=-2$, violating $R>0$. This is a valid counterexample for the specified plant, gain, metric and cost class without state–control cross terms.

The defensible claim is therefore conditional in both directions. Riccati solutions can provide contraction certificates when the metric and decay conditions hold. Some contraction metrics can be interpreted through constructed costs. Neither fact identifies the objective that a golfer actually uses.

## Time-Varying Metrics Need Derivatives and Scale Bounds {#weakness-2-time-varying-metrics-and-the-riccati-equation}

For smooth closed-loop dynamics $\dot x=F(x,t)$, write $A_c=D_xF$. A smooth symmetric positive-definite matrix field $M(x,t)$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H&=\dot M+A_c^\top M+MA_c,\\
\dot M&=\partial_tM+\sum_iF_i\partial_{x_i}M.
\end{aligned}
$$
The material derivative follows the actual closed-loop flow. It is not merely the explicit time derivative of the matrix formula. If $\mathcal H\preceq-2\lambda M$, differential lengths decay at rate $\lambda$, and squared lengths decay at rate $2\lambda$.

When $c_1I\preceq M\preceq c_2I$ uniformly,
$$
\|\delta x(t)\|_2
\leq\sqrt{c_2/c_1}\,e^{-\lambda(t-t_0)}
\|\delta x(t_0)\|_2.
$$
The factor $\sqrt{c_2/c_1}$ is an overshoot bound, not a change in the asymptotic exponent. For a time-dependent certified rate, replace $\lambda(t-t_0)$ by its integral. Over a short swing interval, the prefactor matters: a positive rate need not make the Euclidean bound smaller than its initial value before impact.

The earlier critique's scalar example used $\dot x=-x$ and $M(t)=e^{2t}$. Here
$$
\dot M+2(-1)M=0.
$$
The weighted squared length is constant. No positive contraction rate satisfies the inequality, so the example is not a paradox in contraction theory.

A different scalar example shows why uniform scale matters. Set $\dot x=x$ and $M(t)=e^{-4t}$. Then $\mathcal H=-2M$ and the weighted norm decreases, although $x(t)=e^tx(0)$ grows. The metric tends to zero, destroying a uniform lower bound. Its condition number is exactly one at every time. Reporting condition number alone would miss the problem completely.

For a nonlinear region, contraction of finite distances requires more than testing the nominal trajectory. One must keep the relevant connecting curves and solutions within the verified domain, or use appropriate completeness and invariance hypotheses. Integrating a differential inequality along those curves can establish a finite-separation result; contraction is not inherently restricted to infinitesimal errors. [Manchester and Slotine](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03144) formulate the uniform metric assumptions and this connection through Riemannian distance.

## A Coordinate Representation Can Express an Intrinsic Result {#weakness-3-coordinate-free-claims-vs-coordinate-dependent-reality}

Writing a tensor in coordinates does not make its geometric statement false or non-intrinsic. The relevant question is whether all components transform consistently. A metric is a covariant $(0,2)$ tensor; its matrix changes while the squared length it represents remains the same.

For a smooth time-independent coordinate change $z=\phi(x)$ with invertible $J=D\phi(x)$,
$$
\delta z=J\delta x,\qquad
M_z=J^{-\top}M_xJ^{-1}.
$$
Along the flow, the variational matrix transforms as
$$
A_z=\dot J J^{-1}+JA_xJ^{-1}.
$$
The earlier critique omitted $\dot J J^{-1}$ for nonlinear changes and later used the wrong metric transformation. The simpler similarity formula applies to a constant linear change, or at a fixed point where the relevant moving term vanishes.

Differentiating the transformed metric cancels the extra moving-frame terms:
$$
\dot M_z+A_z^\top M_z+M_zA_z
=J^{-\top}\mathcal H_xJ^{-1}.
$$
Therefore the contraction inequality transforms by congruence and is preserved. Congruence preserves the sign of a quadratic form, not its raw eigenvalues. Resetting $M_z$ to the identity would choose a different metric rather than transform the original one.

For an explicit nonlinear check, take $\dot x=-x$ and $z=x+x^3$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
J&=1+3x^2,\qquad \dot J=-6x^2,\\
A_z&=-1-\frac{6x^2}{1+3x^2},\qquad M_z=J^{-2},\\
\dot M_z+2A_zM_z&=-2J^{-2}=-2M_z.
\end{aligned}
$$
The same intrinsic rate survives. Uniform comparison to a particular Euclidean norm is a separate global question because a diffeomorphism may have unbounded distortion. On a compact nonsingular region, suitable Jacobian bounds provide the needed comparison.

A task map $h:Q\to X$ may instead be noninvertible. Its pullback has coordinate expression $M_q=J_h^\top M_xJ_h$. This form is positive definite only when $J_h$ is injective on the tangent directions under consideration. A redundant three-dimensional configuration mapped to two task coordinates leaves a null direction; the pullback alone is then a seminorm on the full configuration tangent space. It cannot certify contraction of all hidden state directions.

A mathematical metric choice also does not change the physical basin of a fixed closed-loop system. It changes the certificate and perhaps the region or rate that can be proved. A controller redesigned using that metric may change the physical dynamics. Keeping those two actions separate prevents geometric language from being mistaken for a mechanism that generates forces.

## Biomechanical Hypotheses Need Identifiable Mechanisms {#weakness-4-biomechanical-applications-rest-on-unvalidated-assumptions}

### Low-Dimensional Data Do Not Identify a Unique Neural Objective

An EMG factorization, a joint covariance eigenspace, a controller's input subspace and a contraction metric are different objects. Their dimensions, units and dependence on the task must be stated before comparing them. A synergy matrix $W$ does not determine a unique metric $M(W)$ without an additional musculoskeletal dynamics model, input policy, state definition and metric-selection rule.

[Kutch and Valero-Cuevas (2012)](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002434) construct mechanical explanations for low-dimensional activation patterns. Their work motivates controlling for biomechanical and task constraints; it does not disprove all neural synergy hypotheses. Likewise, the absence of contraction terminology in a cited paper is not evidence that its findings contradict every contraction-based model.

The proposed hypothesis that people maximize contraction rate needs an explicit objective and constraints. Without limits or penalties, increasing feedback gain can make a simplified model appear increasingly contractive while ignoring effort, delay, saturation, noise and tissue loading. Even the scalar overdamped mechanical equation shows that more damping does not monotonically improve the slow decay rate: for large damping $d$, the slow root approaches $-k/d$.

A useful study would predeclare the measured task errors, a model that predicts perturbation responses, physiological and actuator bounds, a metric convention, and competing policies. It would then test predictions on held-out perturbations and subjects. Fitting an arbitrary metric or cost separately to each observed swing and reporting a favorable rate is not an independent test of the organizing principle.

### Additive LQG Is Not Every Stochastic Motor-Control Model

For fully observed linear dynamics with additive process noise,
$$
dx=(Ax+Bu)dt+G\,dW_t,
$$
and an expected quadratic cost, use the value form $V=x^\top Sx+c(t)$. The diffusion contribution to the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation is $\operatorname{tr}(SGG^\top)$, independent of $x$ and $u$. It changes the scalar value term, while the control Riccati equation remains the deterministic one under these assumptions.

In the corresponding partially observed additive Gaussian problem, the controller acts on an estimated state. The LQR gain can be independent of noise covariances while the estimator gain and the complete observation-to-action law depend on them. Saying that noise does not affect the controller without this distinction is misleading.

Control-dependent diffusion changes the optimization. For example, terms $D_i u\,dW_i$ contribute
$$
u^\top\left(\sum_iD_i^\top SD_i\right)u
$$
to the value generator, changing the effective quadratic coefficient of $u$. One cannot apply the additive-noise separation argument unchanged.

[Todorov and Jordan (2002)](https://www.nature.com/articles/nn963) explicitly adapt their motor-control simulations to multiplicative noise, filtered neural commands and delayed noisy measurements. Their telescopic-arm example relates a control subspace to the rank of a feedback matrix. It does not establish that empirical EMG synergies are eigenvectors of a control Gramian, nor that golfers maximize a contraction rate.

Risk-sensitive exponential costs are another problem class. Any added Riccati term must be derived with the precise cost normalization, risk parameter and diffusion model. A positive quadratic noise term cannot be inserted into the additive LQG control equation and justified merely by calling noise destabilizing.

Deterministic contraction also does not erase the variability driven by fresh independent disturbances. For
$$
dx=-a x\,dt+g\,dW_t,\qquad a>0,
$$
the variance satisfies $\dot p=-2ap+g^2$ and tends to $g^2/(2a)$. Two trajectories driven by exactly the same noise can have a contracting difference while independent trials retain a nonzero spread. A claim about repeatability must specify which stochastic comparison is intended.

## The Critique's Proposed Data Were Not Observations {#weakness-5-experimental-comparisons-lack-statistical-rigor-and-controls}

The earlier critique supplied replacement robot trials, standard deviations, $p$-values, metric-condition ranges, warm-start iteration counts and LQR-tree performance comparisons. It did not provide data or executable experiments supporting them. Those numbers are withdrawn. Adding plausible-looking uncertainty estimates to unsupported means cannot create evidence.

The historical reference's robot and cartpole tables are likewise not used as validated results here. Without traceable runs and raw observations, it is inappropriate to infer that the experiments were single-trial, that a baseline was poorly tuned, or that a proposed algorithm achieved the reported advantage. The correct finding is that the record does not establish those facts.

A comparative study should use a common task-space error definition, units, perturbations and resource constraints. Each controller may have its own mathematical certificate, but measuring every controller in a separately selected favorable metric is not a fair empirical comparison. Report physical outcomes in a shared metric and certificate diagnostics separately. Tuning effort, available state information, actuation limits, solver tolerances, initialization and stopping criteria should be comparable and disclosed.

The statistical unit must match the claim. Repeated swings from one participant are not independent participants. Paired controller runs should retain the pairing; uncertainty in a performance difference cannot generally be reconstructed from separate marginal intervals. Effect sizes, uncertainty and out-of-sample behavior are more informative than a $p$-value alone.

### A Clearly Labeled Confidence-Interval Example

As a mathematical illustration, suppose there were 94 successes in 100 independent Bernoulli trials. A two-sided 95% Wilson interval is approximately $[0.875,0.972]$. For a hypothetical 100 successes in 100 trials it is approximately $[0.963,1]$, not a zero-width interval. These are calculations from assumed counts, not recovered cartpole results. The [NIST Wilson construction](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section2/prc241.htm) inverts the score test:
$$
\frac{\hat p+z^2/(2n)
\;\pm\;z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n+z^2/(4n^2)}}
{1+z^2/n},
\qquad z=1.959964.
$$
The approximate coverage depends on the sampling assumptions. Neither interval means that the fixed true probability has a frequentist 95% probability of lying inside this particular realized interval. A lower bound near 0.963 also does not mean the system is guaranteed to succeed on 96.3% of every future batch.

### Mechanical and Computational Units Matter

A 5 N load is a force. An impulse is a force integral with units N s, so its waveform or duration is needed to determine the momentum change. A recovery estimate $3/\lambda$ refers to reducing a norm bound by about 95% only when the bound has unit prefactor, constant rate and no continuing disturbance. For a prefactor $C$ and target relative tolerance $\epsilon$, the corresponding sufficient time is $\log(C/\epsilon)/\lambda$, provided the assumptions continue to hold.

A cartpole state mixes translation, angle and their rates. A spherical Gaussian or Euclidean success ball needs declared coordinate scaling; otherwise its numerical size has no consistent physical meaning. A sampled finite-horizon success set is not automatically a basin of attraction, and its volume depends on the chosen state coordinates and measure.

No universal state-dimension cutoff or $O(n^4)$ runtime law is assigned to semidefinite optimization here. Cost depends on the number and size of constraints, parameterization, sparsity, solver and required accuracy. Warm starts can be tested, but their benefit must be measured at comparable residuals. SOS methods and LQR-trees also require their own numerical and dynamical assumptions; they should not be described as exact because they use a particular optimization class.

## A Penalty Is a Search Device {#weakness-6-contraction-constrained-ddp-has-unverified-assumptions-theorem-41}

A large quadratic penalty can discourage a violated contraction constraint without enforcing it exactly. The one-dimensional problem
$$
\min_u\;(u-1)^2+\mu\max(u,0)^2
$$
penalizes violation of $u\leq0$. For every finite $\mu>0$, its minimizer is $u=1/(1+\mu)>0$. Even exact global optimization leaves a violation. This counterexample is sufficient to reject the earlier blanket claim that a sufficiently large finite penalty certifies feasibility.

The critique's proposed threshold involving an eigenvalue of $\partial\mathcal C/\partial u$ was not derived; that derivative need not even be a symmetric square matrix. Its claimed basin radius also omitted metric derivatives, policy variation and domain invariance. Those formulas are withdrawn rather than promoted to conjectures with an unsupported appearance of precision.

A useful separation is to let trajectory optimization search for a candidate, then verify a certificate for the actual implemented feedback. The certificate must include the integration or sample convention, input constraints and the domain on which the derivative bound holds. A finite grid of negative residuals does not alone prove a between-grid or neighborhood inequality.

### What a Neighborhood Bound Would Need

Define the continuous-time residual
$$
\mathcal R(x,t)=\dot M+A_c^\top M+MA_c+2\lambda M.
$$
Suppose the nominal residual obeys $\mathcal R(x^*(t),t)\preceq-\eta I$, and a verified operator-norm bound gives
$$
\|\mathcal R(x,t)-\mathcal R(x^*(t),t)\|_2
\leq L\|x-x^*(t)\|_2
$$
throughout a declared tube. Then any radius $r<\eta/L$ lying within that tube preserves a strict negative residual when $L>0$. This is a bound on the residual field, not just on the Hessian of the open-loop plant. If $L=0$, the residual is constant across the verified spatial domain.

Even this inequality is only part of a certificate. One must also establish that the relevant trajectories and connecting curves remain in the tube, that the metric stays uniformly definite, and that the control remains feasible. Perturbations may activate saturation, change contact mode or leave the model's valid region. A finite-horizon tracking tube does not establish an infinite-horizon basin without a continuation or terminal argument.

Repeatedly resolving a finite-horizon problem does not automatically supply that continuation. Receding-horizon claims require compatible terminal conditions or another stability argument, recursive feasibility, and treatment of the policy changes between solves. The local optimization's stationarity conditions do not establish any of these by themselves.

## Decay Rates, Mechanical Energy and Contact Need Separate Proofs {#weakness-7-missing-proofs-and-unjustified-mathematical-leaps}

### Discrete Time Has Its Own Rate Convention

For discrete LQR, the optimal gain and Riccati recursion give
$$
A_{c,k}^\top S_{k+1}A_{c,k}
=S_k-Q_k-K_k^\top R_kK_k.
$$
Consequently $V_{k+1}=V_k-\delta x_k^\top(Q_k+K_k^\top R_kK_k)\delta x_k$. If $S_k\succ0$ and
$$
Q_k+K_k^\top R_kK_k\succeq(1-\rho)S_k,
\qquad 0<\rho<1,
$$
uniformly, then $V_k\leq\rho^kV_0$. Length decays as $\rho^{k/2}$. For sample duration $\Delta t$, the equivalent length rate is $-\log\rho/(2\Delta t)$; squared length has twice that rate. If the bound gives $\rho=0$, it describes a one-step collapse in the stated metric rather than a finite logarithmic rate.

The earlier critique called a bound using $Q_k$ alone invalid because it omitted $K_k^\top R_kK_k$. Since the omitted term is positive semidefinite, dropping it can give a weaker but valid bound. A weaker sufficient estimate is not a mathematical error. Time-varying factors also require a product or a uniform upper bound; one cannot silently iterate a different $\rho_k$ as if it were constant.

### Endpoint Inertia Is Not a Full Error-State Metric

For an ideal constant-coefficient mechanical error model,
$$
m\ddot e+d\dot e+ke=0,
\qquad m,d,k>0,
$$
the physical energy $E=(m\dot e^2+ke^2)/2$ satisfies $\dot E=-d\dot e^2$. At $e\ne0$, $\dot e=0$, energy is positive and its derivative is zero. Therefore $\dot E\leq-2\lambda E$ cannot hold for any $\lambda>0$ at that state, regardless of the positive gain choices. The failure is in this particular strict energy inequality; it does not imply the damped system is unstable.

An endpoint inertia matrix has the dimension of velocity space. The error state $(e,\dot e)$ has twice that dimension. A full quadratic certificate needs a matrix on that full state, often with position–velocity cross terms. For a constant Hurwitz state matrix $A_e$, one can solve $A_e^\top P+PA_e=-Q_e$ with $Q_e\succ0$ to obtain such a certificate, then determine its rate from the metric inequality.

Critical damping does not justify the earlier exact rate claim. For $m=k=1,d=2$ and $(e(0),\dot e(0))=(1,0)$,
$$
\begin{bmatrix}e(t)\\\dot e(t)\end{bmatrix}
=e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1+t\\-t\end{bmatrix}.
$$
The Jordan polynomial prevents a uniform bound $C e^{-t}$ with finite $C$ for all time. Any smaller positive exponential rate can be accommodated by a suitable prefactor; the spectral boundary rate itself is not an attained quadratic contraction rate.

For configuration-dependent inertia, the complete mechanical equations can contain terms that cancel the inertia derivative in an energy balance. Variable inertia alone does not invalidate trajectory tracking, and constant task inertia does not require every physical configuration to be fixed. The review must inspect the actual model and feedback cancellations. Gain variation, imperfect cancellation and moving targets introduce additional terms that must remain in the derivative.

### A Common Flow Metric Does Not Cover Every Hybrid Event

A common positive-definite quadratic metric satisfying all flow inequalities is sufficient for the corresponding continuous-state switched linear system under the stated switching assumptions. Searching for that common metric with fixed matrices and a fixed rate is an LMI feasibility problem. General difficulty results for switched-system stability do not make this particular convex search nonconvex, nor does an infeasible search prove the system unstable.

Resets require additional conditions. At a scheduled differentiable reset $x^+=r(x^-)$, the differential map is $D r$. For a transverse state-triggered event, the saltation matrix $\Xi$ also accounts for event-time variation. A nonexpanding event requires
$$
\Xi^\top M^+\Xi\preceq M^-.
$$
The applicable event map, guard, reset and regularity assumptions must be stated; a reset Jacobian alone generally misses event-time sensitivity.

As a simple scheduled example, let $\dot x=-x$ between resets and $x^+=2x^-$ every 0.1 time unit. Each flow contracts in $M=1$, but the per-cycle multiplier is $2e^{-0.1}>1$, so the repeated process grows. If jumps have a norm gain bound $\gamma$, the combined estimate contains $\gamma^N e^{-\lambda t}$ after $N$ events. Growth can sometimes be offset by sufficient flow contraction and dwell time. A common metric is a useful sufficient construction, not a necessary condition for every stable hybrid motion.

Golf impact makes this distinction operational. A pre-impact certificate says nothing by itself about the variation of the outgoing ball state or a post-impact body state. Contact geometry, event timing and the reset law belong in the transfer from incoming swing variation to the measured result.

## From a Mathematical Certificate to a Golf-Swing Argument {#weakness-8-ambiguity-in-definitions-and-terminology}

Use the terms according to their roles. A Riemannian metric measures tangent vectors. A contraction metric additionally satisfies a dynamical inequality. A Riccati value matrix comes from a declared optimization problem and serves as a contraction metric only when the extra conditions hold. A numerical residual is evidence about the implemented calculation; a domain certificate is an argument extending that calculation across a specified set.

The question for the swing is not whether every joint deviation can be made to disappear. Consider a terminal output $y=h(x(T))$. For a fixed terminal time, its first-order sensitivity to an initial perturbation is
$$
\delta y\approx D h(x^*(T))\,\Phi(T,t_0)\delta x(t_0),
$$
where $\Phi$ is the closed-loop state-transition matrix along the nominal motion. At a state-triggered impact, replace the fixed-time derivative by the appropriate event-sensitive map. A direction that is task-null now may matter later; a direction that remains large in joint space may still have little effect on the chosen terminal output.

This connects several parts of the physical investigation. Geometry sets Jacobians and lever arms. Inertia and stored energy determine how forces change motion. The available muscle forces, delays and contacts restrict feasible corrections. Feedback changes perturbation evolution. Event geometry converts the delivered state into an outcome. Measurement and model uncertainty determine how confidently that chain can be inferred from data.

A strong argument states which links are mechanical identities, which are properties of a chosen controller, and which are empirical hypotheses. Full-state contraction is one sufficient way to control error growth. Task-specific finite-horizon bounds, orbital or transverse stability, stochastic performance and robust constraint satisfaction can answer different questions. None should be dismissed merely because it does not prove the strongest contraction claim.

The revised reference supplies a technically bounded construction. The remaining scientific task is to build and test models whose assumptions, perturbations and outputs correspond to the movement being studied. The criterion for progress is a more accurate, reproducible prediction of how the swing works.

## In Layman's Terms

A model can explain how a correction propagates through the body without proving that a golfer's nervous system uses that exact correction strategy. It can also show that two swings become more similar in a chosen measure while some physical differences remain important at impact.

Changing the units or coordinates should preserve the same physical conclusion when everything is transformed consistently. Changing the importance assigned to different errors is a modeling decision. Changing muscle forces or feedback changes the motion itself. Keeping those three actions distinct helps the mathematics explain the mechanism.

The earlier review was right to demand evidence, but some of its replacement formulas and example results were wrong. A rigorous review must meet the same standard as the article it reviews: derive the claim, name its limits, and report only observations that actually exist.

## Critics' Comments

### Does This Demand an Unnecessarily Strong Certificate?

No single certificate is required for every question. A short-horizon delivery prediction may be useful without global contraction. The claim should match the proof: a local tube, a finite-time sensitivity bound or a measured success rate can each be valuable when its domain and uncertainty are stated. None automatically establishes the others.

### Does Constructing an Inverse-Optimal Cost Explain Human Behavior?

A constructed cost can explain how a controller fits an optimization framework. If the cost is chosen after observing the controller, that fit alone does not establish why a human selected it. Comparing predeclared objectives through independent predictions makes the inverse problem informative.

### Can Useful Engineering Continue Before Every Hypothesis Is Validated?

Yes. Candidate metrics and penalties can guide design, and simulations can reveal counterexamples or suggest experiments. Their value comes from a clear record of assumptions, numerical checks and predictive limits. A promising design method can be presented honestly while empirical validation remains open.
